deck.title: S3 — Simple Storage Service
deck.analogy: S3 is an infinite valet parking garage for files: hand over the object, get a claim ticket (the key), and get the whole file back — you can't edit it while parked, only replace it.

subtopics.title: The two "special" classes and their exact signals

Who can get in: access controls

cards.front: What kind of storage is Amazon S3, and how do you change part of an object?

back.answer: An object store; you can't edit bytes in place — you replace the whole object.
back.explanation: Unlike a disk (EBS) or shared network filesystem (EFS).
back.mnemonic: Valet garage: you can't change the engine while it's parked.

cards.front: S3 bucket names: unique at what scope, and where does a bucket live?

back.answer: Globally unique across all of AWS; the bucket itself lives in one region you choose.

cards.front: Maximum size of a single S3 object?

back.answer: 5 TB (bucket capacity is unlimited).

cards.front: When is S3 multipart upload recommended vs required?

back.answer: Recommended over 100 MB; required over 5 GB.
back.explanation: A single PUT caps at 5 GB.

cards.front: What durability does S3 promise, and does it vary by storage class?

back.answer: Eleven 9s (99.999999999%), same across every class.
back.explanation: Classes differ in cost, availability and retrieval speed.

cards.front: S3 Standard: retrieval time, minimum storage duration, use case?

back.answer: Milliseconds; no minimum; frequently accessed hot data.

cards.front: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: retrieval time, minimum duration, use case?

back.answer: Milliseconds; no minimum; unknown/unpredictable access patterns.

cards.front: S3 Standard-IA: retrieval time, minimum duration, use case?

back.answer: Milliseconds; 30 days; infrequent access needing instant retrieval.

cards.front: S3 One Zone-IA: retrieval time, minimum duration, use case?

back.answer: Milliseconds; 30 days; infrequent AND re-creatable data (one AZ only).

cards.front: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval: retrieval time, minimum duration, use case?

back.answer: Milliseconds; 90 days; archive touched ~quarterly but needed instantly.

cards.front: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: retrieval options and minimum duration?

back.answer: Expedited 1–5 min, Standard 3–5 hr, Bulk 5–12 hr; 90-day minimum.
back.explanation: Archive where minutes-to-hours retrieval is OK.

cards.front: S3 Glacier Deep Archive: retrieval options and minimum duration?

back.answer: Standard 12 hr, Bulk 48 hr; 180-day minimum. Cheapest class.

cards.front: What are the three filters for choosing the most cost-effective S3 storage class?

back.answer: 1) Access frequency picks the family; 2) retrieval-time requirement eliminates classes; 3) minimum storage duration. Cheapest survivor wins.

cards.front: S3 Filter 1: which class family matches each access frequency?

back.answer: Daily/constant → Standard; monthly-ish → IA; few times a year → Glacier; unknown → Intelligent-Tiering.

cards.front: Data needed within milliseconds, archived — can Glacier still be the answer?

back.answer: Yes, Glacier Instant Retrieval; milliseconds only kills Flexible and Deep Archive.

cards.front: Retrieval deadline is 8 hours and Glacier Deep Archive is cheapest. Pick it?

back.answer: No — Deep Archive can never deliver faster than 12 hours; any deadline under 12 hr disqualifies it.

cards.front: Why does S3 Standard win for data kept under 30 days?

back.answer: Every cheaper class bills a minimum duration (IA 30, Glacier Instant/Flexible 90, Deep Archive 180 days).
back.explanation: Delete early and you pay the minimum anyway.

cards.front: When is S3 One Zone-IA the correct choice?

back.answer: Only when data is re-creatable or a secondary copy (e.g. regenerable thumbnails, replicas, secondary backups).
back.explanation: Data sits in a single AZ — lose the AZ, lose the data; ~20% cheaper.

cards.sourceHeading: The two "special" classes and their exact signals

cards.front: What extra fee does S3 Intelligent-Tiering charge?

back.answer: A monitoring fee per object.
back.explanation: Millions of tiny objects add up.

cards.sourceHeading: The two "special" classes and their exact signals

cards.front: Which objects does S3 Intelligent-Tiering never tier?

back.answer: Objects under 128 KB — they stay at Standard rates.

cards.sourceHeading: The two "special" classes and their exact signals

cards.front: How long does an object pay Standard price before Intelligent-Tiering moves it down?

back.answer: About 30 days of observed inactivity.

cards.sourceHeading: The two "special" classes and their exact signals

cards.front: Access pattern is known (heavy for 30 days, then rare). Use Intelligent-Tiering?

back.answer: No — a lifecycle rule is cheaper and deterministic. IT only when access is unknown/unpredictable/changing.

cards.sourceHeading: The two "special" classes and their exact signals

cards.front: What do S3 lifecycle transition vs expiration actions do?

back.answer: Transition moves objects down the class ladder on a schedule; expiration deletes them.

cards.front: Besides transitions, what cleanup can S3 lifecycle rules do?

back.answer: Delete old versions and abort incomplete multipart uploads.
back.explanation: Incomplete multipart uploads silently cost money forever otherwise.

cards.front: With S3 versioning on, what happens on delete?

back.answer: A delete marker is placed on top; old versions remain, and removing the marker restores the object.
back.explanation: Overwrite creates a new version on top.

cards.front: Can S3 versioning be disabled once enabled?

back.answer: No — only suspended.

cards.front: What does S3 MFA Delete require?

back.answer: The root user's MFA device to permanently delete a version or suspend versioning.

cards.examTip: extra protection against accidental or malicious deletes

cards.front: S3 CRR vs SRR: use cases?

back.answer: CRR: compliance, DR, lower latency in another region. SRR: log aggregation, prod → test copies in same region.

cards.front: What is required for S3 replication?

back.answer: Versioning ON in both source and destination buckets.

cards.front: You enable S3 replication and expect existing objects to copy. What happens, and what's the fix?

back.answer: Only NEW objects replicate; use S3 Batch Replication for existing ones.

cards.front: Encryption at rest vs in transit — and what provides in-transit for S3?

back.answer: At rest = on disk; in transit = over the network, provided by TLS (HTTPS).

cards.sourceHeading: The encryption ladder (sorted by how little you trust AWS)

cards.front: SSE-S3: who holds the key and when to pick it?

back.answer: AWS, fully managed (AES-256); the default on new objects — zero effort.

cards.sourceHeading: The encryption ladder (sorted by how little you trust AWS)

cards.front: SSE-KMS: who holds the key and why pick it?

back.answer: A KMS key you control; audit every key use in CloudTrail, control rotation and who decrypts.

cards.sourceHeading: The encryption ladder (sorted by how little you trust AWS)

cards.front: SSE-C: who holds the key and how is it sent?

back.answer: You supply it on every request over mandatory HTTPS; AWS encrypts but never stores it.

cards.sourceHeading: The encryption ladder (sorted by how little you trust AWS)

cards.front: Client-side encryption for S3: what's the guarantee?

back.answer: You encrypt before upload; AWS never sees plaintext.

cards.sourceHeading: The encryption ladder (sorted by how little you trust AWS)

cards.front: Heavy SSE-KMS traffic hits KMS request limits/costs. Fix and trade-off?

back.answer: S3 Bucket Key — cuts KMS API costs ~99%, but gives a coarser per-object CloudTrail audit trail.

cards.sourceHeading: The encryption ladder (sorted by how little you trust AWS)

cards.front: Question asks to encrypt S3 data in transit; a KMS answer is offered. Pick it?

back.answer: No — in transit means TLS/HTTPS, not KMS.

cards.sourceHeading: The encryption ladder (sorted by how little you trust AWS)

cards.front: How do you enforce HTTPS-only access to an S3 bucket?

back.answer: Bucket policy that Denies requests where aws:SecureTransport = false.

cards.sourceHeading: The encryption ladder (sorted by how little you trust AWS)

cards.front: Default encryption turned on — are existing S3 objects now encrypted?

back.answer: No; encryption applies at write time. Use S3 Batch Operations to re-write existing objects.

cards.sourceHeading: The encryption ladder (sorted by how little you trust AWS)

cards.front: What does S3 Object Lock provide?

back.answer: WORM (Write Once, Read Many): objects can't be deleted or overwritten for a retention period.

cards.front: Requirements for enabling S3 Object Lock?

back.answer: Versioning must be on, and it can only be enabled at bucket creation time.

cards.front: Object Lock Compliance mode: who can delete during retention?

back.answer: Nobody — not admins, not even root.

cards.front: Object Lock Governance mode: who can delete during retention?

back.answer: Users with a special bypass permission.

cards.front: S3 Legal Hold: who can delete and for how long?

back.answer: No one, indefinitely — no expiry, stays until explicitly removed.

cards.front: "Even the root user cannot delete" — Governance or Compliance mode?

back.answer: Compliance, never Governance.
